title: A Reasonable Request for Data and Coding Transparency | Open Research Bulletin
content: Abstract:  Not long ago, I had disparate experiences engaging with two different publications. The first was from a research group I knew and liked. Their article included results that were aligned with what I already knew, but I had a few queries about the analysis. As the data were ‘available on reasonable request’, I promptly made such a request. Although the first author wrote to explain some of the findings to me, they did not share their data and I could not confirm the results. In contrast, the second article was published by a group that I had known to be under scrutiny, and I admit that initially I was critical of the results. However, as their data and analysis scripts were published and accessible (in this case, on the Open Science Framework), I was able to not only confirm the results but also conclude that they had reported them conservatively. In these cases, data (un-)availability influenced my confidence in the research. The inconsistent experiences I have had with data availability emphasise the importance of improving the openness of data in research.

title: Data Management Planning for Open and Reproducible Research | Open Research Bulletin
content: Abstract:  The term Data Management Plan (DMP) can elicit reluctance, scepticism and sometimes even an eye roll from overworked and overstretched researchers, who can view it as an unwelcome administrative burden. In reality, a well-considered DMP is an incredibly valuable project document that underpins open and reproducible research, supporting future reuse by both the research team and others. As the volume and complexity of research data continue to increase, researchers benefit from clear, practical approaches to data storage, security and sharing. This article outlines the core elements of an effective DMP, pitfalls to avoid and how DMPs enable Open Research through responsible data sharing and long-term preservation. It also highlights tools and support available to help researchers create DMPs that are useful throughout the project and beyond.

title: Open Research Data: A Practical Way Forward for Researchers | Open Research Bulletin
content: Abstract:  The UK Reproducibility Network's STAR study examined how 21 UK universities are supporting open research data and found that, while significant progress has been made in policies, infrastructure and support, sharing research data is still not routine in many disciplines. The report argues that researchers should be given structured opportunities to consider the benefits, costs and feasibility of open data at the start of projects, helping them make informed decisions, plan resources effectively, and avoid unnecessary burdens while supporting more sustainable and meaningful open research.

content: Abstract: Introduction: Green Open Access requires authors to submit appropriate versions of journal articles to a repository; the challenge for researchers is to remember to perform this task after the primary work of the publication process is done. This case study at Brock University Library shows how it is possible to bootstrap these types of submissions by crafting meaningful publishing narratives through a collection of clever Open Access Week initiatives. Literature Review: The literature review assesses the existing scholarly material on Open Access outreach efforts and touches on Open Access in the Canadian context. It explores the dynamics of self-archiving with Green Open Access and the use of institutional repositories. The existing literature on wielding open data as a tool to serve libraries is discussed, and the potential of these tools to support librarian advocacy work is examined. title: How policy is reshaping open access: everything, everywhere, all at once - Research Consulting
content: "There’s a growing consensus from governments and funders around the world that publicly funded research should be published openly and preferably openly immediately. Where policymakers diverge is on the mechanism for achieving immediate open access (OA). That divergence is leading to a regionally fragmented publishing sector that creates a strategic problem for publishers: the funding routes they relied on are being withdrawn, and one global model no longer fits every market. In principle, none of this is new. Publishers have run differentiated regional strategies for years, but the pace and the stakes have changed. It also sits alongside other policy fronts moving just as fast, from how AI systems use and help produce scholarly content to questions of copyright and verification. Those issues deserve separate treatment; here, we’re focusing specifically on the rapidly changing policy and funding environment around open access."

title: Securing the digital future of open social sciences and humanities research - Research Information
content:
"New partnerships are formed, communities emerge, and innovative services are developed as a result. Yet forging collaboration is only the beginning. How do successful initiatives move beyond project formation and become sustainable parts of the research ecosystem?

The answer to that question lies within OPERAS’s journey towards becoming a European Research Infrastructure Consortium (ERIC) a legal framework established by the European Commission to provide robust governance and a financially sustainable foundation for pan-European research collaboration.

OPERAS (Open scholarly Communication in the European Research Area for Social Sciences and Humanities) is a European collaboration created to strengthen open scholarly communication in the social sciences and humanities (SSH), bringing together publishers, libraries, researchers and infrastructure providers from across Europe. Through the newly launched OPERAS-PRIME project, the infrastructure is preparing for the next stage of its development, with the aim of achieving ERIC status by late 2027 or early 2028."

title: Who Needs National Journals? Dissemination Strategies in Canadian Scholarly Communication | The Canadian Journal of Information and Library Science
content: Abstract: The dominance of English-language journals marginalizes national and local scholarly publications. Focusing on Canada’s bilingual (English and French), community‑oriented and Open Access‑rich journal ecosystem, this study uses comprehensive data to ask who relies on Canadian journals, how language and research focus affect reach, and what that reveals about balancing local relevance with global visibility. Drawing on two major bibliometric databases (OpenAlex and Dimensions), we show that Canadian journals play a key role as venues for the dissemination of locally relevant research while also contributing to the global infrastructure for scholarly communication. Most articles published in Canadian journals are authored by researchers affiliated with foreign institutions, and most research authored by Canadians is published in journals based outside Canada. We find that Canadian authors are most likely to publish their work in national journals when they are in decision-making roles, when the language of publication is French, or when the topics are locally relevant. title: New UKRN reports highlight opportunities and limits of AI-powered monitoring of research data sharing | UK Reproducibility Network
content: "Two new reports from the UKRN – Working Paper 13: Monitoring Data Availability Statements and FAIR Data Practices in Medical Research Council (MRC)-Funded Research and UKRN Working Paper 14: Monitoring Data Sharing and FAIR Practices with LLMs – provide fresh evidence on how research funders and institutions can monitor data-sharing practices at scale, and what role artificial intelligence is likely to play in the future. Together, the reports address a growing challenge for research policy: how to assess whether publicly funded research data can be found, accessed and reused without relying on costly manual review of thousands of publications every year. While expectations around open research and FAIR data have become increasingly widespread, robust monitoring remains difficult. The first report examines a sample of 2023 publications acknowledging support from the Medical Research Council (MRC). It found that Data Availability Statements (DASs) were present in more than 80% of publications, but only around 59% were judged acceptable against established criteria. title: Popular open-science platform to stop hosting data and code amid funding concerns | Nature
content:
"The co-founder of a prominent open-science platform has announced that funding uncertainties have forced the site to make changes to some of its most popular features.

In a statement released on 11 August, Brian Nosek, executive director of the Center for Open Science (COS) in Charlottesville, Virginia, which runs the Open Science Framework (OSF), announced that the platform will no longer allow researchers to post their code and data after 16 November. Any documents that are already publicly available on the site will remain online. But users will no longer be able to upload new materials in private mode.

The OSF’s preregistration workflow — which allows scientists to post research designs and articles that describe their planned methods and analyses for upcoming experiments — will continue to operate as normal, as will the 14 preprint servers run on the OSF platform."

title: Recommendations for Revising the Open Access Classification System in OpenAlex | Zenodo
content: "The open access (OA) color classification system used by Unpaywall (i.e., Gold, Green, Hybrid, Bronze, and closed) was introduced in 2018 and has since become widely used across the ecosystem, including by Scopus, Web of Science, Dimensions, and numerous funders and institutions worldwide. However, the scholarly communication landscape has changed significantly since these categories were defined and the limits of this system are proving problematic. In particular, the current system struggles with research outputs that are not journal publications, relies too heavily on journal-level policies rather than work-level attributes, conflates business models with access status, and is difficult to accurately operationalize in an environment where journals regularly change the OA status of publications en masse. The OpenAlex Colors Working Group was convened by the OpenAlex Community Advisory Board in January 2026 to evaluate these limitations and recommend a revised framework. title: Biomedical Publishing Metrics as a Barrier to Knowledge Dissemination
content: Abstract:  The Journal Impact Factor (JIF) is an outdated biomedical metric that hinders knowledge dissemination. Relying on citation counts creates a skewed, easily manipulated system with a temporal lag that ignores global equity. Frontline clinicians consume research to improve care but rarely generate citations, meaning the JIF cannot capture real-world clinical utility. To ensure rankings reflect true value, publishers must adopt a multi-dimensional matrix prioritizing usage-based Altmetrics, such as verified downloads and views, to instantly measure global clinical application.

title: Unlocking knowledge: diamond open access publishing - UNESCO Digital Library
content: Diamond Open Access (OA) is an equitable scholarly publishing model that treats knowledge as a digital public good, with no fees for readers or authors. Built on shared infrastructure, open licensing, and community governance, it supports non-profit, academically driven publishing while allowing commercial providers to deliver specific services. Like Open Educational Resources (OER), Diamond OA promotes equitable access, collaboration, and multilingual knowledge sharing. It can strengthen national and institutional Open Access strategies while connecting OER, Open Data, and open research software into interoperable knowledge ecosystems. This brief examines Diamond OA infrastructure and provides practical policy guidance for Member States and institutions.

title: Up Close and Personal with the Trump Administration’s NIH Funding Cuts: An Interview with Sylvia Chou and Alexa Romberg - The Scholarly Kitchen
content: "More than 400,000 US federal employees have left their jobs during the second Trump administration – voluntarily or, in many cases, not. Even taking into account new hires since January 2025, there has been a net loss of 285,000 staff, many of whom had years, if not decades, of experience. Over 10,000 of them were experts in STEM and health fields, with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) especially hard hit, losing more than 1,100 staff – around 10% of its workforce. Among them were Sylvia Chou and Alexa Romberg, who chose to leave the organization as a result of the changes being made under NIH Director Dr Jay Bhattacharya. They were two of the original signatories of the Bethesda Declaration, an open letter to Dr Bhattacharya that expressed serious concerns about the changes being made under his leadership. Sylvia and Alexa are both involved in 27 UNIHTED (Sylvia as a Senior Advisor), an organization that was set up in 2025 as a way to continue supporting the integrity of publicly-funded health research in the United States. title: From access to impact: the gold OA advantage | Springer Nature
content:
"This white paper explores the effect of different routes to OA on the reach and impact of articles in hybrid journals. The data shows that, 8 years on from our first major study into this topic, there is still a substantial advantage for gold OA articles across all disciplines (measured by downloads, citations and Altmetric Attention Score) over both non-OA articles and green OA articles. 4

The analysis of 204,781 articles published in 1,812 hybrid Springer Nature journals in 2023 also shows how gold OA can accelerate the number of downloads over time and the diversity of geographic readership, leading to faster impact and greater equity in access."

title: Gold OA reaches record 44pc share of global research output - Research Information
content:
"Gold open access (OA) articles reached their highest-ever share of global research output in 2025, accounting for 44% of all journal articles, reviews and conference papers published worldwide.

Nearly two million research articles were published through gold OA during the year, making it the principal driver of immediate, freely available access to research, according to the latest release of the STM Open Access Dashboard.

The Dashboard, which tracks the uptake of different routes to OA between 2015 and 2025, shows that gold OA has quadrupled over the past decade."

title: Open Access Library and Information Science (LIS) Journals Indexed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ): An Analytical Study | Annals of Library and Information Studies
content: Abstract: The study examines the trends and current status of Open Access (OA) research journals listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) in the field of Library and Information Science (LIS) from 2003 to mid-2026. It investigates the profile of OA LIS journals, publishing trends, publishing practices, open access policies, licensing practices and journal scope through thematic analysis of keywords. The study identified 231 OA LIS journals published in 32 languages by 200 publishers across 55 countries globally. The study adopted a descriptive research approach and data were collected from the DOAJ and verified through the official journal websites where required. The collected data were compiled, organised, tabulated and analysed using Microsoft Excel. The findings provide insights into the growth of LIS journals, geographical distribution, publishers, language profile, publication mode, peer-review practices, article processing charges (APCs), copyright ownership, Creative Commons licensing, self-archiving policies, digital preservation mechanisms, Digital Object Identifier (DOI) availability and other publishing infrastructure adopted by OA LIS journals.
